own_scenes.desc: Vuelto al underground, el techno necesitaba vinilo barato y rápido y se reconectó con los restos de la industria discográfica de Detroit. Archer, la última planta de prensado de Míchigan (fundada en 1964), resistió los años flacos y sobrevivió al CD gracias a las decenas de sellos de techno. Ron «Motown» Murphy, dueño de la mayor colección de Motown del mundo, abrió en 1989 National Sound (luego Sound Enterprises) para vender discos usados; May y Atkins descubrieron su viejo torno y empezó a cortar más de mil caras al año, con mensajes en los surcos finales (idea suya para Plus 8 y UR), discos que suenan de dentro afuera y el «locked groove», un bucle infinito que inventó por accidente con «The Rings of Saturn» de Jeff Mills, a 133 1/3 bpm. Su equipo único, con amplificadores caseros, es parte del misterio del sonido de Detroit: «el techno es en cierto modo lo mismo» que el R&B y el soul de graves pesados.

refs.q: “We were contemplating the demise of vinyl. Everybody said vinyl was history,” says Joe. “But we kept the doors open.”
refs.para: The Archer Record Pressing Plant, located in Detroit, is the last remaining business of its kind in Michigan, started in 1964 by Norm Archer. Though these days it’s looked after by Norm’s grandson, Mike, in the “lean years” of the 1980s, Joe Archer (Norm’s son) ran the company. “We were contemplating the demise of vinyl. Everybody said vinyl was history,” says Joe. “But we kept the doors open.” In fact, just as the plant went fully automatic, Detroit’s techno labels grew from the initial three to a few dozen and business at the plant began to pick up. This helped Archer outlast the mainstream’s jump to CDs.
refs.chapter: Cap. 5: Off to Battle: Redefining the Detroit Underground, 1990–1995

refs.q: He jumped up and said, “Do you know what this means?!”
refs.para: I had been noticing that a lot of [techno] was very repetitive—I couldn’t help but notice! I kept thinking about that. Jeff Mills came in and said, “I got a thing here called ‘The Rings of Saturn.’ What can we do different?” I said, “All your stuff is these loops, right? I wonder if I can loop it on a record in one turn—like a ring.” He started writing out the information for his labels like a lot of them would while I was working, and I happened to do it. I didn’t realize that it had to be 133 1/3 bpm for it to work at the time, but his track was 133 1/3 bpm just by accident! I played the loop and Jeff looked up ’cause he noticed that something was supposed to change. It was perfect. “That’s the loop I was telling you about,” I said. He jumped up and said, “Do you know what this means?!”
refs.chapter: Cap. 5: Off to Battle: Redefining the Detroit Underground, 1990–1995

refs.q: Being able to see your records being pressed . . . it’s almost a spiritual thing.”
refs.para: Both Archer and Sound Enterprises benefited from techno’s widening popularity for many years. But ask any of Detroit’s artists and producers and they’ll tell it the other way around. “We needed them,” says Lenny Burden of Octave One. “With Ron [Murphy], you could actually be part of the process—he taught people how to engineer their own records. The same goes for Archer. Being able to see your records being pressed . . . it’s almost a spiritual thing.”
